question: In large language models, how does scaling next-word pretraining actually affect hallucination rates?
guest: Predicting the next word seems very simple, but you have to really internalize a lot of what is going on in the context—the previous words, the syntax, who's saying them—and compress all of that information to predict the next word. If you do this extremely well, you develop a model of what's happening in the world, at least the world captured in text. So even when truth is ambiguous, the model can get an idea of which parts of the internet are reliable and which are not, and make entities, dates, and locations more salient. Now, if a language model is only trained to predict the next word and you say, "Elad traveled to blank," of course it's going to make something up without further context. But with a better understanding of what's happening and more context, it can know that it doesn't know and maybe should ask where he went. So pretraining is about predicting the next word and developing a world model. With those capabilities, you still have to say, "Don't hallucinate." But it will be much easier to control that model if it has a notion of what hallucination even is.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Scaling next-word pretraining reduces hallucinations, but it does not eliminate them, and it changes their character.

Larger models trained on more data absorb more facts, so errors on well-represented knowledge fall steadily. But the objective itself rewards producing a plausible continuation, not saying "I don't know." Theoretical work (Kalai and Vempala, 2024; OpenAI's "Why Language Models Hallucinate", 2025) argues that a well-calibrated next-word predictor must make some errors on arbitrary facts that appear rarely in training, such as an obscure person's birthday. No pattern predicts those facts, so more scale only pushes the boundary outward.

Scale also makes the remaining errors more fluent and confident. Zhou et al. (Nature, 2024) found that larger, more instructable models are less likely to abstain, giving plausible wrong answers where smaller ones would decline.

So scaling lowers the overall rate, but with diminishing returns on long-tail facts. Further reductions mostly come from other sources: retrieval and grounding, post-training that teaches abstention, and evaluations that stop rewarding confident guessing.

This is from memory; I did not run a search to verify the citations.

models.answer: Scaling next-word pretraining reduces hallucinations on well-represented facts, as larger models trained on more tokens memorize broader knowledge and track context more accurately. However, scaling alone cannot eliminate hallucinations and yields diminishing returns in the long tail. Because next-word prediction optimizes for plausible continuation rather than truth or abstention, even a well-calibrated model trained on error-free data faces a statistical lower bound on hallucination tied to the "monofact" rate—the fraction of facts appearing only once in the training corpus. Since real-world knowledge is heavy-tailed, larger corpora continually introduce new rare facts alongside repeated ones, causing long-tail hallucination rates to decay very slowly. Scaling raw pretraining can even increase imitative falsehoods, as larger base models better reproduce common human misconceptions and generate more convincing confabulations when uncertain. Ultimately, pretraining scale shifts hallucinations from common facts toward rarer ones; substantially reducing them further requires external retrieval or post-training that rewards abstaining over guessing.

noweb.answer: Scaling next-word pretraining reduces hallucinations on well-represented facts, as greater parameter count, data, and compute allow models to store more world knowledge and make fewer errors on common topics. However, scaling pretraining alone cannot eliminate hallucinations and alters them in two key ways. First, on questions involving popular misconceptions, larger base models can exhibit inverse scaling—becoming more likely to repeat widespread human falsehoods because they fit noisy web distributions more faithfully. Second, next-token cross-entropy loss optimizes statistical plausibility rather than truth, inherently rewarding calibrated guessing over abstention whenever facts appear rarely or only once in the training corpus. Consequently, larger pretrained models hallucinate less often on frequent knowledge, yet still inevitably fabricate long-tail facts, doing so more fluently and authoritatively than smaller models. While pretraining scale raises the ceiling of what a model knows, meaningfully curbing remaining hallucinations requires post-training interventions—such as alignment to express uncertainty, abstention tuning, or external retrieval—rather than scale alone.

Scaling pretraining reduces hallucinations, but not evenly, and it can't drive them to zero on its own.

Bigger models trained on more data make fewer factual errors overall, especially on frequently seen facts and on tasks with learnable patterns like grammar or arithmetic. Accuracy still drops steeply for long-tail knowledge: Kandpal et al. (2023) found it tracks how often a fact appears in the pretraining data.

The theory explains why errors persist. Kalai & Vempala (2023) and Kalai et al. (OpenAI, 2025) argue that a well-calibrated next-word predictor must hallucinate on arbitrary facts that show up rarely, such as a birthday mentioned once. The hallucination rate on those facts is roughly bounded below by the fraction of facts that appear only once in training. More scale doesn't change that statistical limit.

Scale can also make some errors worse. TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2021) found larger models repeated popular misconceptions more fluently. On the plus side, larger models are better calibrated about what they know (Kadavath et al., 2022), which post-training and evaluations that reward abstaining can use to cut confident fabrication. Moreover, as models grow more fluent, their errors often sound more confident and convincing. Cutting hallucinations further therefore requires post-training that rewards calibrated uncertainty and external grounding like retrieval, rather than pretraining scale alone.
